title: A Refresh Interval Does Not Fully Specify a Refresh Schedule: Learning-Rate-Dependent Placement in Kronecker-Preconditioned Language Model Training

paper.title: A Refresh Interval Does Not Fully Specify a Refresh Schedule: Learning-Rate-Dependent Placement in Kronecker-Preconditioned Language Model Training
paper.abstract:
Abstract Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers recompute a cached curvature
eigendecomposition only periodically, and implementations and adaptive
methods control this through the refresh frequency . We show that frequency leaves part of a schedule free: at a fixed number of
refreshes, when they occur changes held-out loss at the same
compute. Training
GPT-style models with the Mousse optimizer across model sizes, we move the middle
refreshes of a four-refresh schedule while fixing the first and last. On FineWeb the two placements exchanged rank as the learning rate rose
(later placement was better at low rates, earlier placement at high ones),
so a single-learning-rate comparison can report either ranking. The
reversal held under controls including the published optimizer internals,
and placement still mattered at the published refresh density. The
learning rate at which the preference flips fell with model size,
consistent with a held-out smaller model, and shifted with training length.
A spectral-width staleness score predicted the same ranking at every
learning rate and missed the reversal.
Refresh schedules should be reported in full and compared across the
learning rates at which they will be used.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: (a) The two schedules. Both perform four refreshes and share their first and last refresh step, and only the two middle refreshes differ. (b) Seed-mean difference τ \tau in endpoint held-out negative log-likelihood (NLL), later schedule minus earlier, against the matrix learning rate (FineWeb, 350M). Positive values mean earlier placement is better. λ × \lambda_{\times} marks the interpolated sign change, and the grey band is the tie tolerance. Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers ( Gupta et al., 2018 ; Anil et al., 2020 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) are increasingly competitive for neural-network and language-model training ( Kasimbeg et al., 2025 ) , but their curvature factorization is expensive, so practical implementations compute it only intermittently and reuse the cached result in between. The standard control on this cost is the refresh interval, and recent methods adapt that interval to a staleness signal ( Eschenhagen et al., 2025 ; Nam and Ahn, 2026 ) . Both treat a schedule as determined by how often refreshes occur. A refresh frequency fixes how many factorizations are computed and leaves open the steps at which they run. The same number of refreshes can be placed differently over training, and each placement decides which cached curvature is applied to which updates. Moving a refresh costs the same compute, because the same eigendecompositions run at different steps. We isolate this choice by holding the refresh count and the first and last refresh steps fixed and moving only the middle refreshes. On FineWeb the same two schedules exchanged rank as the learning rate rose. Later placement gave lower loss at small learning rates and earlier placement at large ones (Figure 1 ). A comparison made at a single learning rate therefore reports whichever ranking that rate selects. This is the confound documented for comparisons between optimizers ( Choi et al., 2019 ; Sivaprasad et al., 2020 ) , here inside one optimizer’s schedule space.

sections.heading: Experimental design.
sections.text: All experiments use Mousse ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , a curvature-augmented Muon optimizer whose factored-curvature eigensystem is recomputed only at refresh steps, on GPT-style models of 64M to 929M parameters trained in a short-horizon regime on six single-domain corpora, with FineWeb as the primary corpus (§ 4.1 ).

sections.heading: Findings.
sections.text: Placement preference reverses with the learning rate (§ 4.2 ). Across intermediate placements, the lowest-loss placement moved earlier as the learning rate rose. The reversal survives controls, and a uniform schedule beats both. It held under controls for warmup, weight decay, the auxiliary learning rate and the published Mousse internals, and placement still changed loss at the published refresh density. An equal-budget uniform schedule beat both mirrored schedules on most corpora, so the mirrored pair serves as a probe of how schedules are compared, and the uniform schedule is the better choice among the three. The boundary moves with scale and horizon (§ 4.3 ). It fell with model size, a held-out smaller model landed inside the band fixed in advance, and it fell faster than the loss-optimal learning rate. Longer training also shifted it. A spectral-width staleness score predicts the same ranking at every learning rate (§ 4.4 ). Most spectral-width change happened before the schedules diverge, so the score tracks early curvature motion and misses the reversal. A schedule comparison therefore needs the full schedule, several learning rates and an equal-budget uniform baseline.

sections.heading: Kronecker-factored preconditioning and its amortization.
sections.text: Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) , Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) and their large-scale refinements ( Anil et al., 2020 ; Morwani et al., 2025 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) precondition matrix-shaped parameters with factored curvature whose eigendecomposition or inverse root dominates per-step cost, so implementations recompute it intermittently. Eigenvalue-corrected K-FAC (EKFAC) ( George et al., 2018 ) and SOAP, which runs Adam in the eigenbasis of Shampoo’s preconditioner ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) , keep a diagonal rescaling current inside a fixed eigenbasis between rebuilds. Standard Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) orthogonalizes the momentum directly, without a cached curvature factorization. Mousse ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) adds Kronecker-factored curvature to a Muon-style update and with it that decision (§ 3.1 ). Appendix F surveys the refresh controls these implementations expose.

sections.heading: Deciding when to refresh.
sections.text: The closest work adapts the refresh frequency to an error signal. Purifying Shampoo triggers an eigenbasis update from a warm-started QR termination bound ( Eschenhagen et al., 2025 ) , and FOAM couples the eigendecomposition frequency and damping to an estimated operator error ( Nam and Ahn, 2026 ) . Both tie timing to cost: a refresh occurs when the error is large enough, so changing when refreshes occur also changes how many occur. Purifying Shampoo further finds that eigenbasis accuracy matters more early in training than late, and leaves open how approximation error affects convergence. § 4.4 tests whether a scalar error signal of this kind predicts the effect of placement. Non-uniform timing is already expressible in practice: Distributed Shampoo exposes a warm-start step alongside its update interval ( Shi et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Evidence on refresh frequency.
sections.text: SOAP reports that recomputing Shampoo’s eigendecomposition less often degrades language-model pretraining, increasingly so as the interval grows, and that SOAP degrades more slowly ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) . Such studies vary how often the factorization is recomputed, while our experiments vary placement at a fixed count (§ 4.2 ). Near the preference boundary the placement effect falls within the tie tolerance, so a comparison made there would report little difference between schedules that separate clearly at other learning rates.

sections.heading: Rankings that depend on how the comparison is run.
sections.text: Optimizer rankings are known to change with the tuning protocol: comparisons at a single hyperparameter point, or under unequal tuning budgets, can reverse conclusions ( Choi et al., 2019 ; Sivaprasad et al., 2020 ; Schmidt et al., 2021 ; Dahl et al., 2023 ) . Recent language-model studies sweep the learning rate for every method ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Semenov et al., 2025 ) and treat scale and data-to-model ratio as axes of the comparison ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , and Wen et al. (2026) also observe that the ranking of two optimizers can flip during learning-rate decay. Optimal learning rates themselves shift with width ( Yang et al., 2021 ) and token horizon ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , the axes against which § 4.3 measures the boundary. We find the same kind of reversal between two equal-cost schedules of one optimizer.

sections.heading: 3.1 Refresh schedules
sections.text: Consider a run of H H optimization steps. A refresh schedule with refresh budget K K (the number of refreshes) is an ordered set S = ( s 1 , … , s K ) , 1 = s 1 < ⋯ < s K ≤ H . S=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{K}),\qquad 1=s_{1}<\cdots<s_{K}\leq H. A refresh is performed before the update at its scheduled step. For update t t , the most recent refresh and the age of its cached factorization are r S ​ ( t ) = max ⁡ { s ∈ S : s ≤ t } , a S ​ ( t ) = t − r S ​ ( t ) . r_{S}(t)=\max\{s\in S:s\leq t\},\;\;a_{S}(t)=t-r_{S}(t). (1) The optimizer we study, Mousse ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , updates its momentum and factored curvature statistics at every step but recomputes the eigendecomposition of the curvature factors only at the steps in S S , applying the cached eigensystem to every update in between. The exact update is given in App. B . Changing S S therefore changes which curvature snapshot is applied during each part of training, while the number of eigendecompositions stays the same. Our primary comparison uses H = 591 H=591 steps with S E \displaystyle S_{E} = ( 1,211,291,561 ) , \displaystyle=(1,211,291,561), S L \displaystyle S_{L} = ( 1,301,381,561 ) . \displaystyle=(1,301,381,561). Here S E S_{E} places the middle refreshes earlier and S L S_{L} later. Both schedules perform four refreshes and share a terminal cache age of 591 − 561 = 30 591-561=30 steps, and their middle refreshes lie within the constant-learning-rate phase of training. Between steps 211 and 290, for example, S E S_{E} applies the cache computed at step 211 while S L S_{L} still applies the cache from step 1. From step 381 to step 560, S L S_{L} applies its step-381 cache while S E S_{E} applies the one from step 291. The pair also differs in total cache age. The sum ∑ t a S ​ ( t ) \sum_{t}a_{S}(t) depends on the refresh gaps and is minimized by even spacing, so the pair differs in total staleness as well as in timing (App. A ). Two designs separate these: the placement landscape of § 4.2 moves the middle pair while keeping its separation fixed, and an equal-budget uniform schedule, which minimizes cumulative age, serves as a reference throughout. Placement also changes the contents of later caches. An earlier refresh alters subsequent parameters, gradients, momentum and curvature statistics, so even the shared final refresh can produce different cached eigensystems on the two trajectories.

sections.heading: 3.2 Placement contrast and preference boundary
sections.text: Let ℓ ⁡ ( S , η , ξ ) \ell(S,\eta;\xi) denote endpoint held-out NLL at matrix learning rate η \eta and seed ξ \xi , with corpus, model size and horizon fixed. Schedules are compared within matched seeds: τ ⁡ ( η , ξ ) \displaystyle\tau(\eta;\xi) = ℓ ⁡ ( S L , η , ξ ) − ℓ ⁡ ( S E , η , ξ ) , \displaystyle=\ell(S_{L},\eta;\xi)-\ell(S_{E},\eta;\xi), (2) τ ¯ \displaystyle\bar{\tau} ( η ) = 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n τ ⁡ ( η , ξ i ) , \displaystyle(\eta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tau(\eta;\xi_{i}), so positive τ \tau favors earlier placement. A contrast inside [ − δ , δ ] [-\delta,\delta] is treated as a tie, and a cell is seed-consistent when every seed receives the same label (earlier better, later better, or tie). The choice of δ \delta is given in § 4.1 . We report individual seed contrasts with each comparison so that effect size and run-to-run variation can be read separately (App. C ). We call the learning rate at an observed sign change the preference boundary λ × \lambda_{\times} , or the crossing. A pair of adjacent grid points whose seed-mean contrasts have opposite signs is a bracket . We estimate λ × \lambda_{\times} by interpolating the seed-mean contrast in log learning rate inside the last bracket of the grid, staying inside the tested grid (Eq. A2 , App. A ). The seed contrasts on either side of λ × \lambda_{\times} show whether the ranking changed consistently across runs.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: All experiments in this section share the setup below.

sections.heading: Models, data and training budget.
sections.text: We trained GPT-style decoder models ( Radford et al., 2019 ) at five sizes from 64M to 929M parameters on six single-domain corpora (FineWeb ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) , and the GitHub, Pile-CC, PubMed Central, arXiv and Books3 subsets of the Pile ( Gao et al., 2021 ) ) and on three FineWeb/GitHub mixtures. FineWeb was the primary corpus. Unless stated otherwise, runs used 65,536 tokens per step for 591 steps under a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Hägele et al., 2024 ) (App. B ). This is a deliberately short regime, between 0.04 0.04 and 0.6 0.6 tokens per parameter and far below compute-optimal training ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . It made dense learning-rate and seed grids affordable at five scales, and § 4.3 varies the horizon directly.

sections.heading: Optimizer.
sections.text: Matrix parameters used Mousse with the schedules of § 3 , and non-matrix parameters used AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) . Our implementation follows the published update but differs in three internals: AdamW rather than Lion ( Chen et al., 2023 ) for non-matrix parameters, a nonnegative eigenvalue correction in place of additive damping, and a m / n \sqrt{m/n} learning-rate adjustment for an m × n m\times n weight matrix (App. B ). A control in § 4.2 restores all three jointly.

sections.heading: Refresh budget.
sections.text: Four refreshes is sparse next to Mousse’s published interval of ten steps, although Shampoo-family deployments report intervals from tens to hundreds of steps ( Anil et al., 2020 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) . A sparse budget leaves long gaps whose placement can be moved over a wide range. § 4.2 also tests larger budgets and the published refresh density.

sections.heading: Learning rates and seeds.
sections.text: The corpus surface, the grid of corpora and matrix learning rates (LRs) at 350M, used five learning rates with two fresh seeds per cell. Controls used three seeds. Independent cohorts, which repeat a model size with fresh seeds, used four. Grids were fixed per experiment and are listed with each experiment (App. B ). A corpus’s tuned learning rate is the grid value that minimizes endpoint NLL for the better of the two mirrored schedules. The uniform reference schedule is ( 1,188,374,561 ) (1,188,374,561) .

sections.heading: Evaluation and tie tolerance.
sections.text: Endpoint NLL was measured on a frozen held-out stream from a shard disjoint from training. The tie tolerance δ = 0.002 \delta=0.002 NLL was registered before the first surface experiment and carried unchanged. It is about one unit of seed-to-seed variation. A run counts as unstable when its endpoint NLL exceeds the best endpoint of its condition by more than a fixed stability margin (App. B ). The conclusions rest on contrasts several times larger (App. C ). Each experiment’s protocol and analyzer were fixed before its data existed (App. B ).

sections.heading: Comparison with uniform placement.
sections.text: At the learning rates tuned for the mirrored pair, an equal-budget uniform schedule outperformed the better mirrored schedule on most corpora (App. C ). The two comparisons answer different questions. The mirrored pair measures how a fixed change in timing interacts with the learning rate, and the uniform schedule measures how far both placements sit from even spacing. Among the schedules tested, even spacing is therefore a strong default at a fixed budget, and the mirrored pair shows how much an uneven choice can shift the ranking between learning rates.

sections.heading: Published refresh density.
sections.text: The larger budgets above keep the long gaps of the sparse pair. A budget-59 pair at the published refresh density instead keeps every gap short, with interval lengths running in opposite directions (Figure 4 a). Placement still changed endpoint loss by several times the tie tolerance, and every seed-consistent cell favored later placement, as the sparse pair does at lower learning rates (Figure 4 b). At low rates the dense contrast was smaller than the sparse one, and its seed spread grew at high rates. The two highest-rate cells were seed-inconsistent, so at this density the data show a placement effect and leave the reversal unresolved.

sections.heading: 4.3 The Boundary Varies with Scale and Horizon
sections.text: Figure 5: (a) λ × \lambda_{\times} against parameter count, one experiment per scale. The dashed line is the fit to the four larger scales, and the square is the held-out 64M measurement. Filled markers are the main estimates, and open markers are independent fresh-seed cohorts (App. D ). (b) The held-out test: the preselected tolerance band, the zero-slope benchmark and the 64M measurement. (c) λ × \lambda_{\times} against the uniform-schedule optimal learning rate λ ref ​ - ​ opt \lambda_{\mathrm{ref\text{-}opt}} . We measured λ × \lambda_{\times} for the same schedule pair on FineWeb at five model sizes, each in a separate experiment with the horizon of § 4.1 . The boundary fell at every step up the ladder (Figure 5 a). To test the trend before seeing the result, we fitted the four larger sizes and fixed a tolerance band around the extrapolated 64M boundary before running 64M. The measured boundary fell inside the band, much closer in log distance to the prediction than to a benchmark in which the boundary stays constant across sizes (Figure 5 b). The band is a preselected acceptance tolerance, and a fit through the independent cohorts alone would have placed the 64M boundary outside it (App. D ). Repeating three sizes with fresh four-seed cohorts tested how precisely each size is located. Every cohort showed the same sign pattern across learning rates, yet each placed its crossing outside the interval of the main estimate, sometimes above it and sometimes below. The spread between cohorts is thus wider than the spread between seeds, so the ladder fixes the direction of the trend more firmly than any single per-size value.

sections.heading: Preference boundary and optimal learning rate.
sections.text: A downward boundary could simply track the loss-optimal learning rate, which also falls with size. We compared the two directly at four scales, using the learning rate that minimizes loss under the equal-budget uniform schedule, λ ref ​ - ​ opt \lambda_{\mathrm{ref\text{-}opt}} . A pre-specified test checked whether the two log–log slopes agree within an equivalence band. The slope difference and its whole seed-bootstrap interval lay outside that band (App. D ). The boundary sat above λ ref ​ - ​ opt \lambda_{\mathrm{ref\text{-}opt}} at every measured scale, and the gap narrowed while staying open (Figure 5 c). Over 64M to 929M, the preference boundary and the loss-optimal learning rate are therefore distinct quantities. The boundary also differs from the stability edge, the lowest unstable learning rate above the uniform-schedule optimum. Across scales the boundary fell faster than the edge, and the ratio between them shrank (App. D ), so the crossing lies below the stability edge at every measured scale.

sections.heading: Training horizon.
sections.text: All model sizes above share one token budget, so size and tokens per parameter vary together along the ladder. At 350M, with the refresh windows scaled in proportion, the reversal remained at twice and four times the original horizon. At eight times the horizon every tested cell favored later placement or tied, which leaves two readings open: the boundary moved above the grid, or the contrast flattened (App. D ). The smaller 64M model lost the effect sooner. By four times the original horizon, every contrast away from the stability edge was within the tolerance. At matched tokens per parameter, 350M crossed while 64M and 124M favored earlier placement at every tested learning rate, so model size affects the contrast beyond its effect on tokens per parameter (App. D ).

sections.heading: 4.4 Spectral-Width Drift Predicts the Same Ranking at Every Learning Rate
sections.text: Figure 6: (a) Normalised spectral-width profiles w ⁡ ( t ) w(t) of the 20-refresh reference runs (FineWeb, five learning rates). The dashed line marks the first step at which the two schedules differ. (b) Top: decomposition of the score contrast Δ ​ I w \Delta I_{w} into D 1 D_{1} and R w R_{w} (Eq. 5 ), in width × \times steps. Bottom: the measured τ \tau of the same cells, in NLL, with the tie band. (c) Δ ​ I w \Delta I_{w} (Eq. 4 ) against measured τ \tau over all 30 cells, with per-corpus fits. Error-triggered refresh rules rest on the idea that a refresh helps once the cached curvature has drifted from the current training state. If that idea explained placement, a measure of accumulated drift should predict which schedule wins at each learning rate. We tested one measurable version, accumulated change in the spectral width of the curvature factors, as a registered prediction. Let w ⁡ ( t ) w(t) be the spectral-width profile of a separately instrumented reference run for the same (corpus, learning rate, seed) cell, which refreshes at a set of probe steps. The statistic aggregates the log ratio of upper and lower eigenvalue quantiles across matrix parameters (App. A ). Both schedules are evaluated on the same reference profile. Using the last-refresh function of Eq. 1 , define I w ​ ( S ) \displaystyle I_{w}(S) = ∫ 1 H | w ⁡ ( t ) − w ⁡ ( r S ​ ( t ) ) | ​ d t , \displaystyle=\int_{1}^{H}\bigl|w(t)-w(r_{S}(t))\bigr|\,dt, (4) Δ ​ I w \displaystyle\Delta I_{w} = I w ​ ( S L ) − I w ​ ( S E ) . \displaystyle=I_{w}(S_{L})-I_{w}(S_{E}). A positive Δ ​ I w \Delta I_{w} means that later placement accumulates more spectral-width mismatch, so the score predicts an advantage for earlier placement. The score is measured in spectral width times training steps. It ranks schedules. The registered test compared the within-corpus rank order of Δ ​ I w \Delta I_{w} with that of the measured τ \tau across learning rates, against frozen targets and a frozen withdrawal threshold (App. E ). Δ ​ I w \Delta I_{w} was positive in every cell, so it predicted earlier placement everywhere, while the measured contrast changed sign on the crossing corpora. From the lowest to the highest learning rate, Δ ​ I w \Delta I_{w} fell in every corpus while the measured contrast rose in all but one. The within-corpus rank correlation was negative on average and positive only in Books3 (Figure 6 c), whose contrast collapses where its runs became unstable. The profiles themselves were stable across seeds (App. E ). The registered prediction was therefore withdrawn.

sections.heading: Source of the score.
sections.text: Most of the spectral-width motion occurred before the two schedules first differ (Figure 6 a). For the primary pair the score has the exact decomposition Δ ​ I w = ∫ 211 301 | w ⁡ ( t ) − w ⁡ ( 1 ) | ​ d t ⏟ D 1 + R w , \Delta I_{w}=\underbrace{\int_{211}^{301}\bigl|w(t)-w(1)\bigr|\,dt}_{D_{1}}+R_{w}, (5) where D 1 D_{1} is the extra exposure to the step-1 reference value under later placement and R w R_{w} collects the signed differences between the remaining intervals (App. A ). D 1 D_{1} accounted for nearly all of the net contrast and often more, and R w R_{w} was negative in all but one cell. Because D 1 D_{1} compares the profile after step 211 with its value at step 1, it mostly records curvature motion that happened before the schedules diverge. Four other registered operationalisations of staleness, including a single-interval drift statistic, a data-freshness gain and a generalisation account, also failed to predict the boundary (App. E ).

sections.heading: Spectral width and the update.
sections.text: Spectral width summarizes eigenvalue spread, while the preconditioned update also depends on the eigenvectors and on the gradient expressed in that basis. Two curvature factors related by a rotation have identical spectral width, but their difference can be large in operator norm (App. A ). The score also measures drift on a common reference trajectory, whereas training applies each cached factor along its own schedule-specific trajectory. Front-loaded curvature motion has also been reported by Gur-Ari et al. (2018) and Cohen et al. (2021) , and early training is known to shape later training ( Achille et al., 2019 ; Frankle et al., 2020 ) .

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that, in short language-model training with Mousse, a refresh interval leaves part of a refresh schedule free: at a fixed budget, where the refreshes fall changes held-out loss, and which placement wins depends on the learning rate, the model size and the training length. Schedules should be compared across the learning rates at which they will be used, because a single learning rate can report either ranking. Adding one learning rate on each side of the tuned rate triples the cost of a single-rate comparison and shows whether the ranking holds near the operating point. An equal-budget uniform schedule makes a useful reference, because two schedules at the same budget can both sit far from even spacing, and a predictor of placement needs more than scalar drift of the curvature spectrum. Over the measured range the boundary fell faster with model size than the loss-optimal learning rate, and the gap between them narrowed (§ 4.3 ). A learning rate tuned or transferred for a larger model therefore sits closer to the boundary, where the two placements are near a tie, so a schedule ranking obtained at one scale should be rechecked after scaling. Our results add a dimension to earlier evidence on refresh timing. SOAP showed that longer refresh intervals degrade training ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) , and our experiments show that, at a fixed number of refreshes, their placement matters as well. Purifying Shampoo found that eigenbasis error matters far more in early iterations than in late ones ( Eschenhagen et al., 2025 ) . Most spectral-width motion in our runs also occurred early, before the two schedules diverge (§ 4.4 ), so the two observations agree that early curvature carries most of the change. Error-triggered refresh rules ( Eschenhagen et al., 2025 ; Nam and Ahn, 2026 ) change when refreshes occur and are usually evaluated at one tuned learning rate, the setting to which these practices apply directly. The natural next measurement records the cached eigenvectors at every refresh and, at each probe step, computes their principal angles to the fresh eigenbasis, weighted by how much of the gradient falls in each direction. Such a score follows each schedule along its own trajectory and sees rotation as well as spread, the two properties the spectral-width score leaves out. Longer horizons and other Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers are the other open tests.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: One optimizer. The reversal is established for Mousse. Restoring its published internals preserved it, but attempts to extend the study to other Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers were inconclusive, and the direction of the effect may differ for other optimizers (App. C ). Short training. Runs use far fewer tokens per parameter than compute-optimal training ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , and the response changes with horizon. Because model size and tokens per parameter vary together, the cross-size boundary is a coarse trend over 64M to 929M. Mechanism. The spectral-width score and other staleness accounts failed to predict the boundary, and measuring eigenvector rotation is left to future work.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: This work measures optimizer dynamics on public pretraining corpora and releases only code, registration protocols and adjudicated statistics. FineWeb is distributed under ODC-By 1.0. The Pile subsets (GitHub, Pile-CC, PubMed Central, arXiv, Books3) are used under the Pile’s terms as a compilation. Books3 contains copyrighted books, and it appears here solely as one of six domain streams for a training-dynamics measurement whose outputs are loss values. Its societal risks are those of language-model pretraining in general, and its practical recommendations concern experimental reporting.

sections.heading: Differences from published Mousse.
sections.text: We implemented the published update: whitening, Newton–Schulz orthogonalization and unwhitening, trace normalization, β = 0.95 \beta=0.95 , α = 0.125 \alpha=0.125 and Frobenius-norm grafting. The intended change is the refresh schedule, which replaces the published uniform interval of ten steps. Three further internals differ: we shift the spectrum as λ ← λ + max ⁡ { 0 , − λ min } + 10 − 10 \lambda\leftarrow\lambda+\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}\}+10^{-10} instead of adding 10 − 5 ​ I 10^{-5}I damping, we apply a m / n \sqrt{m/n} matrix learning-rate adjustment, and we optimize non-matrix parameters with AdamW instead of Lion. App. C restores all three. Arbitrary placement is implemented by setting the refresh interval to a value larger than the horizon and forcing a refresh exactly at the schedule steps. A per-step check verified the age of the applied cache in every run.

sections.heading: Models, evaluation and compute.
sections.text: All models are GPT-style decoders with vocabulary 50,304 and context 1,024: 64M has 12 layers of width 512 and 8 heads, 124M has 12 layers of width 768 and 12 heads, 350M has 24 layers of width 1,024 and 16 heads, 695M has 32 layers of width 1,280 and 20 heads, and 929M has 30 layers of width 1,536 and 24 heads. Every evaluation uses the same 2,097,152-token held-out stream from a shard disjoint from training. A run counts as unstable when its endpoint NLL exceeds the best endpoint of its condition by more than 0.15 0.15 , the stability margin. Each run used one A100-SXM4-40GB from a pool of eight identical devices. Median training time per run at 591 steps, excluding evaluation, was 6.2 (64M), 7.5 (124M), 18.5 (350M), 54.6 (695M) and 55.4 minutes (929M). The experiments comprise 1,973 1{,}973 completed runs and about 920 920 A100-hours of training. Software: PyTorch 2.7.1 ( Paszke et al., 2019 ) , CUDA 12.6, Python 3.11.

sections.heading: Pre-specification and reproducibility.
sections.text: For each experiment, the protocol, learning-rate grid, seeds, decision rule and analysis script were fixed before the experiment ran. Seeds were fresh for every experiment, and results from different experiments were kept separate. Experiments were designed in sequence, each after the results of earlier ones were known. Training is bit-deterministic given the seed: six duplicate configurations in the learning-rate-ratio experiment, run separately and in two cases on different devices, reproduced endpoint NLL exactly. The code, protocols and analysis scripts are provided in anonymized form as supplementary material.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.18695v1 [cs.LG] 13 Oct 2026 A Refresh Interval Does Not Fully Specify a Refresh Schedule: Learning-Rate-Dependent Placement in Kronecker-Preconditioned Language Model Training Xinyu Wang Zhiwei Zhai Affiliation: McGill University The Chinese University of Hong Kong Yu Gu Zijun Yu Sicheng Lyu Jingrui Tian Lei Ding Ziyang Song Xiao-Wen Chang Affiliation: University of Manitoba Ohio University Abstract Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers recompute a cached curvature eigendecomposition only periodically, and implementations and adaptive methods control this through the refresh frequency . We show that frequency leaves part of a schedule free: at a fixed number of refreshes, when they occur changes held-out loss at the same compute. Training GPT-style models with the Mousse optimizer across model sizes, we move the middle refreshes of a four-refresh schedule while fixing the first and last. On FineWeb the two placements exchanged rank as the learning rate rose (later placement was better at low rates, earlier placement at high ones), so a single-learning-rate comparison can report either ranking. The reversal held under controls including the published optimizer internals, and placement still mattered at the published refresh density. The learning rate at which the preference flips fell with model size, consistent with a held-out smaller model, and shifted with training length. A spectral-width staleness score predicted the same ranking at every learning rate and missed the reversal. Refresh schedules should be reported in full and compared across the learning rates at which they will be used. 1 Introduction Figure 1: (a) The two schedules. Both perform four refreshes and share their first and last refresh step, and only the two middle refreshes differ. (b) Seed-mean difference τ \tau in endpoint held-out negative log-likelihood (NLL), later schedule minus earlier, against the matrix learning rate (FineWeb, 350M). Positive values mean earlier placement is better. λ × \lambda_{\times} marks the interpolated sign change, and the grey band is the tie tolerance. Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers ( Gupta et al., 2018 ; Anil et al., 2020 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) are increasingly competitive for neural-network and language-model training ( Kasimbeg et al., 2025 ) , but their curvature factorization is expensive, so practical implementations compute it only intermittently and reuse the cached result in between. The standard control on this cost is the refresh interval, and recent methods adapt that interval to a staleness signal ( Eschenhagen et al., 2025 ; Nam and Ahn, 2026 ) . Both treat a schedule as determined by how often refreshes occur. A refresh frequency fixes how many factorizations are computed and leaves open the steps at which they run. The same number of refreshes can be placed differently over training, and each placement decides which cached curvature is applied to which updates. Moving a refresh costs the same compute, because the same eigendecompositions run at different steps. We isolate this choice by holding the refresh count and the first and last refresh steps fixed and moving only the middle refreshes. On FineWeb the same two schedules exchanged rank as the learning rate rose. Later placement gave lower loss at small learning rates and earlier placement at large ones (Figure 1 ). A comparison made at a single learning rate therefore reports whichever ranking that rate selects. This is the confound documented for comparisons between optimizers ( Choi et al., 2019 ; Sivaprasad et al., 2020 ) , here inside one optimizer’s schedule space. Experimental design. All experiments use Mousse ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , a curvature-augmented Muon optimizer whose factored-curvature eigensystem is recomputed only at refresh steps, on GPT-style models of 64M to 929M parameters trained in a short-horizon regime on six single-domain corpora, with FineWeb as the primary corpus (§ 4.1 ). Findings. Placement preference reverses with the learning rate (§ 4.2 ). Across intermediate placements, the lowest-loss placement moved earlier as the learning rate rose. The reversal survives controls, and a uniform schedule beats both. It held under controls for warmup, weight decay, the auxiliary learning rate and the published Mousse internals, and placement still changed loss at the published refresh density. An equal-budget uniform schedule beat both mirrored schedules on most corpora, so the mirrored pair serves as a probe of how schedules are compared, and the uniform schedule is the better choice among the three. The boundary moves with scale and horizon (§ 4.3 ). It fell with model size, a held-out smaller model landed inside the band fixed in advance, and it fell faster than the loss-optimal learning rate. Longer training also shifted it. A spectral-width staleness score predicts the same ranking at every learning rate (§ 4.4 ). Most spectral-width change happened before the schedules diverge, so the score tracks early curvature motion and misses the reversal. A schedule comparison therefore needs the full schedule, several learning rates and an equal-budget uniform baseline. 2 Related Work Kronecker-factored preconditioning and its amortization. Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) , Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) and their large-scale refinements ( Anil et al., 2020 ; Morwani et al., 2025 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) precondition matrix-shaped parameters with factored curvature whose eigendecomposition or inverse root dominates per-step cost, so implementations recompute it intermittently. Eigenvalue-corrected K-FAC (EKFAC) ( George et al., 2018 ) and SOAP, which runs Adam in the eigenbasis of Shampoo’s preconditioner ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) , keep a diagonal rescaling current inside a fixed eigenbasis between rebuilds. Standard Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) orthogonalizes the momentum directly, without a cached curvature factorization. Mousse ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) adds Kronecker-factored curvature to a Muon-style update and with it that decision (§ 3.1 ). Appendix F surveys the refresh controls these implementations expose. Deciding when to refresh. The closest work adapts the refresh frequency to an error signal. Purifying Shampoo triggers an eigenbasis update from a warm-started QR termination bound ( Eschenhagen et al., 2025 ) , and FOAM couples the eigendecomposition frequency and damping to an estimated operator error ( Nam and Ahn, 2026 ) . Both tie timing to cost: a refresh occurs when the error is large enough, so changing when refreshes occur also changes how many occur. Purifying Shampoo further finds that eigenbasis accuracy matters more early in training than late, and leaves open how approximation error affects convergence. § 4.4 tests whether a scalar error signal of this kind predicts the effect of placement. Non-uniform timing is already expressible in practice: Distributed Shampoo exposes a warm-start step alongside its update interval ( Shi et al., 2023 ) . Evidence on refresh frequency. (2021) , and early training is known to shape later training ( Achille et al., 2019 ; Frankle et al., 2020 ) . 5 Discussion and Conclusion We have shown that, in short language-model training with Mousse, a refresh interval leaves part of a refresh schedule free: at a fixed budget, where the refreshes fall changes held-out loss, and which placement wins depends on the learning rate, the model size and the training length. Schedules should be compared across the learning rates at which they will be used, because a single learning rate can report either ranking. Adding one learning rate on each side of the tuned rate triples the cost of a single-rate comparison and shows whether the ranking holds near the operating point. An equal-budget uniform schedule makes a useful reference, because two schedules at the same budget can both sit far from even spacing, and a predictor of placement needs more than scalar drift of the curvature spectrum. Over the measured range the boundary fell faster with model size than the loss-optimal learning rate, and the gap between them narrowed (§ 4.3 ). A learning rate tuned or transferred for a larger model therefore sits closer to the boundary, where the two placements are near a tie, so a schedule ranking obtained at one scale should be rechecked after scaling. Our results add a dimension to earlier evidence on refresh timing. SOAP showed that longer refresh intervals degrade training ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) , and our experiments show that, at a fixed number of refreshes, their placement matters as well. Purifying Shampoo found that eigenbasis error matters far more in early iterations than in late ones ( Eschenhagen et al., 2025 ) . Most spectral-width motion in our runs also occurred early, before the two schedules diverge (§ 4.4 ), so the two observations agree that early curvature carries most of the change. Error-triggered refresh rules ( Eschenhagen et al., 2025 ; Nam and Ahn, 2026 ) change when refreshes occur and are usually evaluated at one tuned learning rate, the setting to which these practices apply directly. The natural next measurement records the cached eigenvectors at every refresh and, at each probe step, computes their principal angles to the fresh eigenbasis, weighted by how much of the gradient falls in each direction. Such a score follows each schedule along its own trajectory and sees rotation as well as spread, the two properties the spectral-width score leaves out. Longer horizons and other Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers are the other open tests. Limitations One optimizer. The reversal is established for Mousse. Restoring its published internals preserved it, but attempts to extend the study to other Kronecker-preconditioned optimizers were inconclusive, and the direction of the effect may differ for other optimizers (App. C ). Short training. Runs use far fewer tokens per parameter than compute-optimal training ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , and the response changes with horizon. Because model size and tokens per parameter vary together, the cross-size boundary is a coarse trend over 64M to 929M. Mechanism. The spectral-width score and other staleness accounts failed to predict the boundary, and measuring eigenvector rotation is left to future work.
